overview:
Iceland is an island nation floating alone in the North Atlantic, just below the Arctic Circle, about halfway between Norway and Greenland. It is roughly the size of Kentucky, but it holds Europe's largest glaciers, more than 30 active volcano systems, hot springs, geysers, and waterfalls at nearly every turn. The capital, Reykjavik, on the southwest coast, is the northernmost capital city in the world and home to well over half of the country's people.

Only about 390,000 people live in Iceland, fewer than in many mid-sized cities, and they speak Icelandic, a language so little changed that schoolchildren can read the Viking sagas written 800 years ago. Iceland is a parliamentary republic, and its parliament, the Althing, founded in 930, is often called the oldest in the world. Almost all of the country's electricity and heating comes from clean geothermal and hydro power. Fishing built the economy, and tourism now brings in far more visitors each year than Iceland has residents, drawn by the northern lights, glaciers, and volcanic landscapes.
landAndNature: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where two of the Earth's plates pull apart, so the island is literally growing by about two centimeters a year and is riddled with volcanoes. Eruptions are frequent; one in 2010 grounded flights across Europe with ash, and new lava fields formed near Reykjavik in the 2020s. Vatnajökull is the largest glacier in Europe by volume, and ice caps cover about a tenth of the country. Geysers spout boiling water, and the original Geysir gave the word to the world. Waterfalls such as Gullfoss and Dettifoss thunder through canyons. There are no native reptiles, almost no trees, and only one native land mammal, the Arctic fox, but millions of puffins nest on the cliffs, whales feed offshore, and sturdy Icelandic horses graze the moss-covered lava.
peopleAndCulture: Icelanders have no family names in the usual sense; a child's last name is the father's or mother's first name plus son or dóttir, and everyone is listed by first name in the phone book. The country reads and writes more books per person than almost anywhere, and a flood of new titles appears each Christmas. Foods include lamb, fresh fish, skyr, a thick yogurt-like dairy dish, and hot dogs from a famous Reykjavik stand, while fermented shark is eaten mainly at midwinter feasts. Nearly every town has a geothermal swimming pool and hot tubs where neighbors chat. Soccer is loved, and Iceland's team reached the quarterfinals of Euro 2016. Strongman contests, chess, and handball are national passions, and singer Björk and the band Sigur Rós made Icelandic music famous.
history: Norse settlers, mostly from Norway, arrived around 870, led according to the sagas by Ingólfur Arnarson, who built a farm where Reykjavik now stands. In 930 chieftains founded the Althing, an assembly held each summer at Thingvellir, and in the year 1000 Iceland adopted Christianity by a vote there. Poets wrote the sagas, some of the greatest medieval literature, in the 1200s. Iceland came under Norwegian and then Danish rule from 1262, and centuries of cold, plague, and a catastrophic volcanic eruption in 1783 kept it poor. Independence movements grew in the 1800s, home rule came in 1904, and Iceland became a fully independent republic on June 17, 1944. Britain and the United States occupied the island during World War II. Iceland joined NATO in 1949 and weathered a severe banking crash in 2008.
funFacts: Iceland has no mosquitoes at all, one of the very few places on Earth where that is true.
About 90 percent of Icelandic homes are heated with hot water pumped straight from the ground.
Iceland's parliament, the Althing, was founded in 930 and is often called the oldest parliament in the world.
The country has no army, and its police officers usually do not carry guns.
Some Icelanders say they cannot rule out the existence of elves, and road projects have been rerouted around rocks said to be elf homes.
